Getting started with rpact

Friedrich Pahlke and Gernot Wassmer

2026-10-30

Source: vignettes/rpact_getting_started.Rmd
rpact_getting_started.Rmd

Confirmatory Adaptive Clinical Trial Design and Analysis

rpact supports the design, simulation, and analysis of confirmatory clinical trials, from standard fixed-sample planning to group sequential and adaptive methods. Sample size and power planning and simulation are available for continuous, binary, survival (time-to-event), and count data endpoints.

Functional Range

Sample size and power planning

  • Standard fixed-sample designs without interim analyses
  • Classical group sequential designs with planned interim analyses
  • Sample size and power calculations for
    • means (continuous endpoints)
    • rates (binary endpoints)
    • survival (time-to-event) endpoints with flexible recruitment and survival-time options
    • count data endpoints

Simulation and adaptive trial design

  • Power and operating-characteristic simulations for means, rates, survival data, and count data
  • Assessment of adaptive sample size or event-number reassessment based on conditional power
  • Multi-stage adaptive hypothesis testing based on the combination testing principle
  • Assessment of treatment selection strategies in multi-arm trials, including multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) settings for means, rates, and survival endpoints
  • Simulation and analysis methods for population enrichment designs with means, rates, and hazard ratios

Analysis and trial conduct

  • Confirmatory analysis for means and rates in one-arm and two-arm trials, and for survival endpoints in treatment comparisons
  • Multi-arm and population enrichment analysis for means, rates, and survival endpoints
  • Analysis of general estimates and standard errors supplied through getDataset(est = ..., se = ...)
  • Support for fixed-sample designs, classical group sequential designs, and adaptive multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) designs based on the inverse normal or Fisher combination test
  • Automatic boundary recalculation during a trial using alpha-spending approaches, including under- and over-running

Learn to use rpact

We recommend three ways to learn how to use rpact:

  1. Use RPACT Cloud: demo.rpact.cloud
  2. Use the Vignettes: rpact.org/vignettes
  3. Book a training: rpact.com

RPACT Cloud

RPACT Cloud provides guided, browser-based access to selected rpact functionality, including study design, sample size calculation, simulation, and reporting, without requiring users to write R code: demo.rpact.cloud.

Vignettes and function reference

Practical examples and tutorials are available at rpact.org/vignettes. For function arguments, return values, and examples, see the function reference.

User Concept

Workflow

  1. Create a fixed-sample, group sequential, or adaptive design.
  2. Compare alternative designs with getDesignSet().
  3. Calculate the required sample size with, for example, getSampleSizeMeans(), or evaluate power for a specified sample size with getPowerMeans().
  4. Assess operating characteristics and adaptation strategies using simulation, for example, getSimulationMeans().
  5. Prepare aggregated trial data with getDataset() and analyze them with getAnalysisResults().

Planning example

Plan a two-arm trial with a continuous endpoint, a one-sided significance level of 0.025, 90% power, and three analyses at 50%, 75%, and 100% of the planned information. Assume a mean difference of 0.5 and a common standard deviation of 1.

library(rpact)
design <- getDesignGroupSequential(
    kMax = 3, informationRates = c(0.5, 0.75, 1),
    alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.1, sided = 1, typeOfDesign = "OF"
)
sampleSize <- getSampleSizeMeans(
    design = design, groups = 2, alternative = 0.5,
    stDev = 1, allocationRatioPlanned = 1
)
summary(sampleSize)

Sample size calculation for a continuous endpoint

Sequential analysis with a maximum of three looks (group sequential design), one-sided overall significance level 2.5%, power 90%. The results were calculated for a two-sample t-test, H0: mu(1) - mu(2) = 0, H1: effect = 0.5, standard deviation = 1.

Stage 1 2 3
Planned information rate 50% 75% 100%
Cumulative alpha spent 0.0021 0.0105 0.0250
Stage levels (one-sided) 0.0021 0.0097 0.0215
Efficacy boundary (z-value scale) 2.863 2.337 2.024
Efficacy boundary (t) 0.631 0.415 0.309
Cumulative power 0.2928 0.6960 0.9000
Number of subjects 86.9 130.4 173.8
Expected number of subjects under H1 130.9
Stopping probability 0.6960
Efficacy stopping probability by stage (under H0) 0.0021 0.0084
Efficacy stopping probability by stage 0.2928 0.4033

Legend:

  • (t): treatment effect scale

For a design without interim analyses, use getDesignFixed() instead.

Analysis example

The following illustrative data represent two independent groups at each of three stages. Sample sizes, means, and standard deviations are stage-wise: each entry describes only the new observations collected in that stage. The sample sizes are chosen for illustration, independently of the planning result above.

trialData <- getDataset(
    sampleSizes1 = c(40, 20, 20), sampleSizes2 = c(40, 20, 20),
    means1 = c(0.2, 0.3, 0.5), means2 = c(0, 0, 0),
    stDevs1 = c(1, 1, 1), stDevs2 = c(1, 1, 1)
)
analysisResults <- getAnalysisResults(
    design = design, dataInput = trialData, directionUpper = TRUE
)
summary(analysisResults)

Analysis results for a continuous endpoint

Sequential analysis with three looks (group sequential design), one-sided overall significance level 2.5%. The results were calculated using a two-sample t-test, equal variances option. H0: mu(1) - mu(2) = 0 against H1: mu(1) - mu(2) > 0.

Stage 1 2 3
Planned information rate 50% 75% 100%
Cumulative alpha spent 0.0021 0.0105 0.0250
Stage levels (one-sided) 0.0021 0.0097 0.0215
Efficacy boundary (z-value scale) 2.863 2.337 2.024
Cumulative effect size 0.200 0.233 0.300
Cumulative (pooled) standard deviation 1.000 0.992 0.991
Overall test statistic 0.894 1.288 1.914
Overall p-value 0.1869 0.1001 0.0287
Test action continue continue accept
Conditional rejection probability 0.0252 0.0337
95% repeated confidence interval [-0.459; 0.859] [-0.196; 0.663] [-0.020; 0.620]
Repeated p-value 0.3515 0.1719 0.0338
Final p-value 0.0314
Final confidence interval [-0.016; 0.602]
Median unbiased estimate 0.294

If the available summaries are cumulative, use the corresponding cumulative prefixes, such as cumulativeSampleSizes1, cumulativeMeans1, and cumulativeStDevs1. For survival data, cumulative event counts and log-rank statistics are commonly used; see getDataset() for the required inputs. Analysis results and the availability of confidence intervals depend on the chosen design and endpoint; see getAnalysisResults() for details.

Focus on Usability

The terms survival and time-to-event refer to the same endpoint type here. The corresponding function names use the suffix Survival.

The most important rpact functions have intuitive names:

  • getDesign[Fixed/GroupSequential/InverseNormal/Fisher]()
  • getDesignCharacteristics()
  • getSampleSize[Means/Rates/Survival/Counts]()
  • getPower[Means/Rates/Survival/Counts]()
  • getSimulation[Means/Rates/Survival/Counts]()
  • getSimulationMultiArm[Means/Rates/Survival]()
  • getSimulationEnrichment[Means/Rates/Survival]()
  • getDesignConditionalDunnett() for adaptive two-stage multi-arm designs
  • getDataset()
  • getAnalysisResults()
  • getStageResults()

RStudio / Positron / VS Code / Eclipse: auto code completion makes it easy to use these functions.

R generics

Result objects support familiar R functions such as print(), summary(), plot(), as.data.frame(), names(), and length(). The available methods depend on the object class; see the corresponding function reference.

Utilities

Several utility functions are available, e.g.

  • getAccrualTime()
  • getPiecewiseSurvivalTime()
  • getNumberOfSubjects()
  • getEventProbabilities()
  • getPiecewiseExponentialDistribution()
  • survival helper functions for conversion of pi, lambda and median, e.g., getLambdaByMedian()
  • testPackage(): installation qualification on a client computer or company server (see Installation Qualification of rpact)

Validation

For organizations using rpact in FDA/GxP-regulated environments, RPACT offers support and formal validation documentation for use on validated corporate computer systems. The documentation can be customized and licensed for exclusive use by your company to support applicable regulatory requirements.

The validation documentation also contains the personal access data required to run the full test suite for installation qualification with testPackage().

Contact RPACT to learn more.

RPACT Connect

RPACT Connect provides access to insights, downloads, and premium support for users and organizations working with RPACT software: connect.rpact.app.

About

rpact is free of charge and open source, licensed under LGPL-3. It implements a broad range of methods described in the monograph by Wassmer and Brannath (2025). Formal validation documentation is available to customers and supporting members through the RPACT service level agreement.

RPACT GmbH develops Statistical Tools for Drug Development. We develop and support R packages, Shiny applications, and cloud-based tools for clinical research, with services covering software development, validation, technical support, consulting, and training.

Our products include rpact and RPACT Cloud. We also maintain and support crmPack, the open-source package for dose escalation trial design, simulation, and analysis.

For more information, visit www.rpact.com.
